title: PC-Relative Addressing and the Branch Offset Arithmetic
quickIdea: PC-relative means the effective address is the program counter plus a signed offset. The only thing to get right is which value of the PC is added - usually the address of the next instruction.
remember: Effective address = PC + offset. The offset is signed, so a branch can go backwards.
The PC used is the address of the next instruction (the one after the branch), not the branch's own address, on RISC designs that increment during fetch.
If the offset is in bytes and instructions are 4 bytes, divide the address difference by 4 to get the offset a word-indexed field would hold - and do not divide if the field is byte-indexed.
The offset is position independent: move the whole program and every offset is unchanged, which is what makes the mode relocatable.
Branch targets, not data, are its main use, which is why it is the one mode whose offset field is signed.
The reach is small and local - a signed 16-bit byte offset is +-32 KB - which is why long jumps need a register form.

example.prompt: A RISC machine has 4-byte instructions. A beq at index i+3 targets the instruction at index i, and the offset field is in bytes relative to the next instruction. What is the offset?
example.work: If the beq is at address X, the next instruction is at X + 4. The target is at X - 12. Offset = target - next = (X - 12) - (X + 4) = -16.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2017 Set 1 asks exactly this for a four-instruction sequence and the answer is -16. GATE CSE 1998 Q.1.19 asks the design consequence - which mode permits relocation without any change in the code - and PC-relative is the accepted answer. The two together are the whole of what the mode is for.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Same machine, but the offset field is in words rather than bytes. What is the offset for the same branch?
variations.why: One word is 4 bytes, so -16 bytes is -4 words. Reading whether the field counts bytes or words is the first step of every such question.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is the PC value used the next instruction's address rather than the branch's own?
variations.answer: Because the PC has already been incremented by the time the offset is added - the fetch unit advanced it, so that is the value available.
variations.why: It is a hardware fact, not a convention chosen for convenience. On a machine that does not pre-increment, the offset is measured from the branch itself, and a question will say which.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A loop body is 40 KB long and the machine has a signed 16-bit byte offset. What happens?
variations.answer: The backward branch cannot reach the loop head: 40960 exceeds the +-32768 reach, so the compiler must invert the branch and add an unconditional jump.
variations.why: Reach is a real constraint on real code, and it is the reason branch relaxation exists in assemblers.

trap.what: Measuring the offset from the branch instruction's own address.
trap.why: The PC has already moved on. Using the branch's address makes every answer wrong by exactly one instruction length.
trap.counterexample: In the 2017 Set 1 sequence, measuring from the beq itself gives -12 rather than -16. Both are plausible-looking numbers, which is why the question is a good discriminator.

check.question: A 4-byte-instruction machine has a branch at address 1000 with offset -8, measured from the next instruction. Where does it go?
check.explanation: Next instruction at 1004, minus 8 gives 996, which is two instructions back from the branch.
